brief: SocGen's Albert Edwards compares the AI boom to the 1997 Asian crisis, built on weak total factor productivity (TFP) data: Apollo's Slok shows AI investment and equity valuations rising while TFP stays flat, calling it capital deepening rather than a technology shock, so the productivity payoff remains forecast, not observed. BofA's Hartnett and Fed officials Goolsbee and Warsh have flagged the same gap. Edwards draws the direct parallel to 1990s Asia, where Krugman argued poor TFP exposed the "miracle" as capital misallocation before the 1997 collapse. On capex quality, net investment stays flat after depreciation despite gross AI spending, and Goldman's own math needs about $920 billion of annual revenue just to cover depreciation under a zero-ROIC case, rising to trillions through 2030 to hit target returns; OpenAI's revenue reportedly came in $20 billion below prior signals. Edwards argues the real break point isn't productivity but credit: AI capex needs the same bond buyers now being tested by a selloff rotating across France, Japan, the UK and the US, with AI issuers adding chip debt and one AI IPO already showing equity worth less than debt.
